posts.text:
I spent some time this week reading through what SAP announced at its Connect event in Las Vegas, and the thing I keep turning over isn't a product so much as a sentence. SAP's product chief Manoj Swaminathan described the company's new Joule Work layer as "AI on apps as opposed to AI in apps." I think that small distinction will matter more than the launch itself.

For years the assumption has been that AI would live inside each application — a copilot in your ERP, another in your expense tool, another in procurement. What SAP is now betting on is the opposite: an agentic layer that sits above all of them and does the switching for you. SiliconANGLE's coverage framed it as a control plane rather than a copilot, and noted Salesforce and ServiceNow are chasing the same idea.

What makes me cautious is that SAP itself is hedging. Swaminathan called the autonomous enterprise "a journey for customers, not an overnight transformation," and defined autonomy as giving people the tools to observe and trust agents before delegating to them. That reads less like a victory lap than an honest admission that trust is the bottleneck, not capability.

The finance detail that caught me: SAP says Joule Work is already running across 110,000 of its own employees, with roughly 20% productivity gains in finance, HR and procurement. Impressive if it holds — though a vendor's internal numbers are the easiest kind to produce. My guess is the real test is whether a CFO's team trusts an agent to touch revenue recognition, not whether it can draft a variance narrative.

Worth a read:

https://news.sap.com/2026/10/sap-connect-sap-puts-autonomous-enterprise-to-work/

SAP made its autonomous enterprise generally available this week at Connect, and underneath the branding there are a few numbers worth separating from the noise.

The headline claim is that Joule Work — SAP's new agentic layer that runs across apps rather than inside them — is live across 110,000 SAP employees, delivering about 20% productivity gains in finance, HR and procurement. Treat that as a vendor's internal pilot, not an independent benchmark. A 20% lift on well-structured back-office tasks is plausible; whether it survives contact with a messy multi-entity close is the open question.

More telling to me is the pricing shift. According to SiliconANGLE, SAP is moving agent usage onto a consumption model — "AI units" metered per inference, with visibility into usage. That changes the CFO's calculus: agentic automation stops being a fixed subscription line and becomes a variable cost that scales with how much you actually delegate. Budgeting for that is a different muscle than budgeting for seats.

The capability stack is real. SAP points to a knowledge graph it says spans 7M+ data fields, 70+ models, and ISO/IEC 42001 certification for the governance layer. That matters because SAP's genuine moat isn't the model — it's the structured understanding of ERP semantics that general-purpose models from OpenAI or Anthropic don't carry.

The honest caveat is SAP's own. Its product chief called this "a journey, not an overnight transformation," and much of the Autonomous Suite is slated to arrive through early 2027. So the fair read is a credible direction with a long tail of delivery, not a finished product.

https://siliconangle.com/2026/10/06/sap-expands-joule-into-an-agentic-work-layer-as-autonomous-enterprise-goes-live/
https://news.sap.com/2026/10/sap-connect-sap-puts-autonomous-enterprise-to-work/

The line that stuck with me from SAP's Connect announcements this week came from the CFO of Morgan Foods, quoted in SAP's own writeup: "Our superpower will come from people on top of agents." Not the agents themselves — the people on top of them.

It's a small phrase in a launch crowded with bigger ones. SAP put its autonomous enterprise into general availability, debuted an embedded payments product called SAP Pay, and introduced Joule Work, a layer its product chief described as "AI on apps as opposed to AI in apps" — meaning the AI sits above your ERP, travel and procurement tools and works across them rather than living inside each one.

But that CFO's framing is the part I think finance leaders should hold onto. The easy story about agentic finance is subtraction — fewer people, a faster close, less of the month-end grind. The harder and more accurate story is about where human judgment moves. If an agent drafts the flux analysis and reconciles the intercompany entries, a person's value is no longer in producing the number; it's in knowing when the agent is confidently wrong.

SAP seems to half-agree. It defined autonomy not as delegation but as giving people the tools to observe and trust agents first, and admitted the whole thing is a journey, with much of the suite arriving through early 2027. My guess is the firms that do well won't be the ones who deploy the most agents, but the ones who work out what "on top of agents" actually means for a finance team's day.
